area-of-study-1-western-classical-tradit.d: Area of Study 1: Western Classical Tradition 1650-1910
terms: Broken-chord accompaniment pattern in the left hand, named after Domenico Alberti and widely used by Mozart.
Sensitive style associated with C.P.E. Bach, marked by sudden mood changes, ornamentation and expressive nuance.
Mid-eighteenth-century style favouring elegance, light textures and clear cadences as a reaction against baroque complexity.
Texture with a clear melody supported by chordal accompaniment, dominant in classical-era music.
Balanced phrase construction in regular four-bar and eight-bar units, creating clear question-and-answer structures.
Late-eighteenth-century expressive style featuring minor keys, syncopation and dramatic gestures, found in Haydn's symphonies of the 1770s.
Drum-kit emphasis with the snare struck on beats 2 and 4 of the bar, the rhythmic foundation of most pop and rock grooves.
Short, instantly memorable melodic, rhythmic or lyrical idea designed to lodge in the listener's memory, usually placed prominently in the chorus.
Studio technique of capturing each part on a separate track so performances can be overdubbed, edited, balanced and mixed independently.
Short repeated instrumental figure, often on guitar, bass or keyboard, that gives a pop or rock track its distinctive identity.
Sound processing such as reverb, delay, distortion, EQ and compression used in pop production to shape timbre and create space in the mix.
Standard pop structure alternating storytelling verses with a repeated chorus, often extended by an intro, pre-chorus, middle 8 (bridge) and outro.

area-of-study-3-music-for-media.d: Area of Study 3: Music for Media
terms: Video-game scoring built from loops and layers that change in real time according to the player's location, actions and tension level.
Music that exists inside the story world and can be heard by the characters, such as a radio playing or an on-screen band.
Recurring theme attached to a character, place or idea, transformed in orchestration, harmony or tempo as the drama develops on screen.
Scoring technique in which the music closely mimics on-screen movement, historically associated with animation and physical comedy.
Background score heard only by the audience, supporting dialogue and action by shaping mood without drawing attention to itself.
Planning stage where director and composer watch the edit and decide exactly where each music cue should start, stop and peak.

area-of-study-4-music-for-theatre.d: Area of Study 4: Music for Theatre
terms: Show in which songs and dances are integrated into a scripted dramatic plot (the 'book'), so numbers advance story and reveal character.
Full-company piece, often closing an act, that combines several characters' melodic lines and viewpoints in one musical texture.
Orchestral opening played before the action begins, traditionally a medley previewing the show's main melodies to settle the audience.
Return of an earlier song later in the show, usually altered in lyrics, key or mood to show how the dramatic situation has changed.
Musical with little or no spoken dialogue, where virtually the whole drama is carried in continuous music, as in 'Les Miserables'.
Short repeated accompaniment figure that can loop flexibly under dialogue, holding the music in place until the singer is ready to begin.
Fast, virtuosic 1940s style developed by Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, featuring complex harmony and rapid eighth-note lines.
Chord progression of a tune, which improvisers outline melodically through chord-tone and scale choices.
Improvised chordal accompaniment provided by piano or guitar behind a soloist, supporting and responding to the improvisation.
Main melodic theme of a jazz performance, played at the start and end, with improvisations on its chord changes between.
Style based on scales rather than chord changes, pioneered by Miles Davis on 'Kind of Blue' (1959).
Unequal subdivision of beats where eighth notes are performed with a long-short feel, fundamental to mainstream jazz.

area-of-study-6-contemporary-traditional.d: Area of Study 6: Contemporary Traditional Music
terms: A leader's phrase answered by a group or second player, a structural principle central to many African and other folk traditions.
Sustained pitch or pair of pitches held beneath a melody, characteristic of bagpipe traditions and of the Indian tanpura.
Contemporary artists blend traditional material with jazz, classical, rock or electronic idioms; Piazzolla's tango nuevo fused tango with jazz and classical techniques.
Many folk tunes use modes such as Dorian or Mixolydian rather than the major-minor system, giving them their distinctive colour.
Transmission of tunes and songs by ear rather than notation, producing regional variants and allowing each performer a personal version.
Decorative additions such as slides, grace notes, rolls and mordents with which traditional performers personalise and vary a melody.

The relationship between simultaneous musical layers - monophonic, homophonic or polyphonic - varied by composers to create contrast and shape.

terms: Audible metronome heard through headphones by performers, ensuring synchronisation with picture during recording.
Use of recurring themes associated with characters or ideas, employed by John Williams in the 'Star Wars' (1977) score.
Close synchronisation of music with on-screen action, named after early Disney cartoons of the 1930s.
Music with a visible or implied source within the film world, also called diegetic music.
Pre-existing music placed in an edit as a guide while a composer writes the final score.
Background music that supports on-screen action without drawing attention to itself, shaping mood and pace.

area-of-study-4-popular-music-and-jazz.d: Area of Study 4: Popular Music and Jazz
terms: Computer-produced dance genres including house, techno and drum and bass, developing from late-1980s club culture.
Genre originating in 1970s New York combining rapping, sampling, DJing and breakdancing, founded in the Bronx.
Detroit record label founded by Berry Gordy in 1959, releasing soul hits by The Supremes, Marvin Gaye and Stevie Wonder.
Late-1960s and 1970s style with extended forms and classical influences, exemplified by Pink Floyd and Yes.
Stripped-down, fast and aggressive style emerging 1976-77, led by the Sex Pistols and The Clash in Britain.
Style emerging in mid-1950s America from rhythm and blues and country, popularised by Elvis Presley and Chuck Berry.
A repeating two-bar rhythmic timeline, in 3-2 or 2-3 form, that anchors the parts of an Afro-Cuban ensemble; also the paired sticks that play it.
Afro-Cuban style fusing Spanish-derived song and guitar traditions with African rhythmic practice, featuring call and response and clave-based rhythm.
Music that deliberately blends elements of two or more distinct traditions, such as jazz with Afro-Cuban styles or Western classical with gamelan-inspired sounds.
Debussy evoked the Javanese gamelan in piano works such as 'Pagodes', using pentatonic collections, layered textures and bell-like sonorities.
Combining jazz improvisation and harmony with the grooves and production of other styles, as in Courtney Pine's blends of jazz with hip-hop and soul.
Off-beat accents and conflicting rhythmic groupings, central to fused Afro-Latin styles and a key feature to identify in listening questions.
Rapidly shifting time signatures and irregular accents that destroy a predictable pulse, a hallmark of Stravinsky's rhythmic innovation.
Unconventional ways of playing instruments, such as col legno, multiphonics or bowing behind the bridge, used to expand the palette of sound.
Leaving elements of a piece to chance or to performers' choices within a framework defined by the composer, an approach associated with Cage.
Real-time electronic processing of a performer's sound, such as delay, harmonisation and reverberation, as in Saariaho's 'Petals' for cello and electronics.
John Cage altered the piano's timbre by inserting bolts, screws and rubber between the strings, turning it into a one-player percussion ensemble.
Early twentieth-century style of driving rhythms, harsh dissonance and folk-derived melody, epitomised by Stravinsky's ballet 'The Rite of Spring'.

area-of-study-1-instrumental-music-of-ha.d: Area of Study 1: Instrumental Music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven
terms: Broken-chord left-hand accompaniment pattern that animates harmony beneath a singing melody, ubiquitous in Classical keyboard writing.
Beethoven enlarged Classical forms with longer developments and codas, scherzos replacing minuets, and dramatic dynamic extremes, opening the path to Romanticism.

Genre for two violins, viola and cello in which Haydn led the way, prized for conversational part-writing among equal instruments.

Performance style with unequal long-short quaver pairs, a walking bass on four beats and riff-based call and response between sections.
